x: Ashokan inscriptions fall into three groups: rock inscriptions (major and minor rock edicts), pillar inscriptions and cave inscriptions such as those in the Barabar hills. Copper-plate, coin and mosque inscriptions belong to later periods.
t: Recall the three types of Ashokan inscriptions.

x: Shahbazgarhi is in Kharosthi, Taxila in Aramaic, Kandahar (Shar-i-Kuna) is bilingual in Greek and Aramaic, and Laghman is in Aramaic. The code pairs items in order when List-II repeats, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Recall the script of each north-western edict.

x: James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837 and so became the first scholar to read Ashoka's edicts. Harisena, Ravikirti and Vasula Kavi were ancient court poets who composed inscriptions.
t: Separate modern decipherers from ancient composers.

x: Option C is incorrect: most Ashokan inscriptions are in Brahmi, not Kharosthi. Kharosthi, written right to left, was used only in the north-west, as at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra.
t: Recall which script dominates Ashokan edicts.

x: Rummindei marks Buddha's birthplace, Bhabru (Bairat) shows Ashoka's faith in Buddhism, Kanganahalli has a stone portrait of Ashoka with a queen, and the Kalsi rock edicts are near Dehradun, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Recall the key feature of each site.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Rock Edict XIII records the Kalinga War and Ashoka's remorse over its suffering, which led him to give up military conquest for Dhamma conquest.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: I, II, III and IV are all correct: RE I bans animal sacrifice, RE II arranges medical care for humans and animals, RE XII urges religious tolerance and RE XIII records the Kalinga War and remorse.
t: Recall the theme of each Rock Edict.

x: The Boghaz-Koi inscription (c. 1400 BC, Turkey) names the Vedic gods Indra, Varuna, Mitra and the Nasatyas as witnesses to a treaty. Agni, Soma, Shiva and Buddha are not in it.
t: Recall the four gods named in the treaty.

x: Rudradaman I is the ruler of the Junagadh inscription, Pushyagupta was Chandragupta Maurya's governor who built the lake, Tushasp was Ashoka's governor who added canals, and Rudradaman repaired the Sudarshan Lake, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.
t: Link each governor to his Mauryan king.

x: The Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri near Bhubaneswar is the main source for Kharavela, the Jain king of Kalinga. Rudradaman I is known from Junagadh and Pushyamitra from Ayodhya.
t: Link each inscription to its ruler.

x: All four are correct: Ayodhya with Pushyamitra Shunga, Nanaghat with the Satavahanas, Nashik with Gautamiputra Satakarni and Hathigumpha with Kharavela.
t: Check each pair separately.

x: Both are true: the Sarnath Buddhist image inscription is dated to Kanishka's third year (81 AD), and the Rabatak inscription is in the Bactrian language written in Greek script.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Mughal emperor Akbar moved the Ashokan pillar from Kaushambi to the Allahabad (Prayagraj) fort. Jahangir later added his own Persian inscription to it, which is the common trap.
t: Discriminate Akbar's move from Jahangir's inscription.

x: The Mehrauli Iron Pillar names king Chandra (Chandragupta II), Bhitari records Skandagupta's war with the Hunas, Eran gives the first inscriptional evidence of sati, and Mandsaur records the silk-weavers' guild and Sun Temple, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Recall the key content of each Gupta inscription.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the Mandsaur inscription is tied to the silk-weavers' guild because it records how the guild migrated from Lata (Gujarat) and built a Sun Temple at Dashpur.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: The Sarnath image inscription is 81 AD, Eran 510 AD, Lohnara 630 AD and the Chausath Yogini temple inscription 1323 CE, giving B, C, A, D.
t: Arrange the inscriptions by date.

x: Khalimpur records Dharmapala and the election of Gopala, the Motupalli epigraph lists trade and tariff rates, the Sanjan and Radhanpur plates record Govinda III's victory over Nagabhata II, and Garhmukteshwar shows Balban as helper of the Caliph, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the content of each inscription.

x: I, II, III and IV are all correct: Mahmud Ghazni's bilingual silver coins used Arabic and Devanagari Sanskrit, Ghori's coins showed Lakshmi, Iltutmish added the Caliph's name after recognition, and Alauddin styled himself Sikandar-i-Sani.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: All four are correct: RE I bans animal slaughter, RE II names the southern kingdoms and provides medical care, RE XII preaches religious harmony and RE XIII records Kalinga and remorse.
t: Recall the theme of each Rock Edict.

x: The Bhabru (Bairat) inscription calls Ashoka "Piyadasi Raja" of Magadha and declares his faith in the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha. Param Saugat was Dharmapala's title and Sikandar-i-Sani Alauddin Khalji's.
t: Match the title to the ruler before choosing.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the revenue cut recorded at Lumbini is exactly Ashoka's grant exempting it from bali and lowering the land share (bhaga) from one-sixth to one-eighth.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Rock Edict XII asks people to respect all religious sects and to restrain speech about others' faiths. RE I bans animal sacrifice, RE II covers medical care and RE XIII deals with Kalinga.
t: Recall the theme of each Rock Edict.

x: The Boghaz-Koi inscription in Asia Minor (Turkey) is dated to about the 14th century BC and names Vedic gods, which helps date early Vedic culture.
t: Recall the date of the Hittite-Mitanni treaty.

x: Both are true: the Mauryan-era Sohgaura copper plate orders grain to be stored for times of famine or crisis, and the Mahasthan inscription in Bengal deals with famine relief.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Junagadh belongs to Rudradaman I, Hathigumpha to Kharavela, Ayodhya to Pushyamitra Shunga, and Nanaghat describes Satavahana administration, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Link each inscription to its ruler.

x: The Hathigumpha inscription opens with a salutation to the Jinas and records Kharavela's gifts to Jain monks, showing he followed Jainism.
t: Recall Kharavela's religion.

x: I, II and III are correct: the Rabatak inscription was found in 1993 and is in Bactrian written in Greek script. IV is false because Shravasti is not among the cities it names.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: The Prayag Prashasti lists Mahendra of Kosala (Dakshina Kosala) among the southern kings Samudragupta defeated and released. Gopala was a Pala king, and Nagabhata II a Pratihara.
t: Recall the southern kings in the Prayag Prashasti.

x: The Allahabad pillar carries Ashoka's edicts, the Queen's Edict about Karuvaki, Harisena's prashasti of Samudragupta and Jahangir's Persian inscription, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the four layers of writing on the pillar.

x: Both are true: the Eran inscription of 510 AD is the first epigraphic evidence of sati, recording that the wife of the commander Goparaja burned herself on his pyre.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Vatsabhatti composed the Mandsaur (Dashpur) inscription of the silk-weavers' guild. Harisena wrote the Prayag Prashasti, Ravikirti the Aihole inscription and Vasula Kavi the Sondani inscription.
t: Link each poet to his inscription.

x: Option B is incorrect: the Aihole inscription says Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha's southward advance at the Narmada, not the Krishna. It was composed by Ravikirti and mentions Kalidasa and Bharavi.
t: Check the river named in each statement.

x: The Junagadh inscription is c. 150 AD, the Badami rock inscription is Saka 465 (543 AD), Lohnara is 630 AD and the Chausath Yogini inscription is 1323 CE, giving D, A, B, C. The old key placed Badami first, but Saka 465 converts to 543 AD, after Junagadh.
t: Convert the Saka year to AD by adding 78.

x: Sondani belongs to Yashodharman, the Maukhari copper seal to Sarvavarman, the Chausath Yogini inscription to the Kachchhapaghata king Devapala, and the Gwalior inscription to Mihirakula's rule, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.
t: Link each inscription to its ruler.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I matter for Chola village government because they describe the sabha, its committees and how members were chosen.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: "Al Sultan Zilli Allah" on Muhammad bin Tughluq's coins means "the Sultan is the Shadow of God", stressing the divine standing of the ruler.
t: Translate the key word Zill (shadow).

x: All eight are major rock edict sites: Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra in the north-west, Kalsi, Girnar, Sopara, Dhauli and Jaugada, and Yerragudi in Andhra Pradesh.
t: Recall the major rock edict sites.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: most Ashokan edicts are in Prakrit language and Brahmi script, but a script is only a way of writing and does not cause the choice of language.
t: Discriminate language from script.

x: I, II and III are correct: Ashoka is called Priyadarshi, Piyadasi and Devanampiya Piyadasi. IV is false because "Beloved of the Gods" translates Devanampiya; Piyadasi (Priyadarshi) means "of gracious appearance".
t: Separate the meaning of Devanampiya from Piyadasi.

x: All three, Gujarra, Nittur (Nettur) and Udegolam, name Ashoka personally, as does Maski. Most other edicts use only his titles Devanampiya Piyadasi.
t: Recall the edicts that use the name Ashoka.

x: Both are true: the Rummindei pillar records Ashoka's visit to Lumbini, and the Bhabru inscription is issued by Piyadasi, King of Magadha.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: I, II and III are all correct: Kanganahalli lies in Karnataka on the Bhima River and carries a portrait panel labelled "Ranyo Ashoka".
t: Check each statement separately.

x: "Ranyo Ashoka" means King Ashoka, the phrase is found at Kanganahalli, Kalsi is an Ashokan rock-edict site, and the rock edicts are linked back to Kalsi, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Match the most direct description first.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Rock Edict I says killing for the royal kitchen was first cut down step by step, and this gradual reduction led to its complete stop.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All six are named in Rock Edict II: the Cholas, Pandyas, Satiyaputras, Keralaputras and Tamraparni, which is Sri Lanka.
t: Recall the southern neighbours in Rock Edict II.

x: All five fit Rock Edict XIII: it dates the Kalinga War to the eighth year after coronation (c. 261 BC) and names Greek (Yavana) rulers such as Antiochus.
t: Check each detail against Rock Edict XIII.

x: Both are true: the Sohgaura copper plate comes from Gorakhpur in Uttar Pradesh and is regarded as the earliest known copper plate.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: The Mahasthan inscription comes from Mahasthangarh in Bogura (Bogra), Bangladesh. Gorakhpur is Sohgaura, Girnar is Junagadh and Asia Minor is Boghaz-Koi.
t: Link each place to its inscription.

x: The Junagadh inscription is important for the Sudarshan Lake, is written in Sanskrit, uses Brahmi script and is linked with the Sudarshan Lake, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii.
t: Match language and script first.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the Junagadh inscription is the earliest long Sanskrit inscription and an early Kavya-style work, but using good Sanskrit does not by itself make a text ornate poetry.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: The Hathigumpha inscription records thirteen years of Kharavela's reign, mentions a Nanda ruler (identified as Mahapadmananda) and records extending a canal, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Match the specific item before the general one.

x: I, II and III are all correct: Kharavela ruled Kalinga, and his Hathigumpha inscription records southern victories and refers to a Nanda king.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Both are true: the Ayodhya inscription of Dhanadeva describes Pushyamitra Shunga as having performed two Ashvamedha sacrifices.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: The Nashik inscription of Gautami Balashri calls her son Gautamiputra Satakarni "Ekabrahmana" (unrivalled Brahmana). Sikandar-i-Sani, Param Saugat and Piyadasi Raja are titles of other rulers.
t: Match each title to its ruler.

x: The Nanaghat inscription, issued by Naganika, records Satakarni I's rule, while the Nashik inscription was issued by Gautami Balashri, giving a-ii, b-i.
t: Recall who issued each inscription.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Ekabrahmana means "unrivalled Brahmana", and the Nashik inscription merely records the title; where it appears does not explain its meaning.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: The Sarnath image inscription is at Sarnath and belongs to Kanishka; the Rabatak inscription was found in Afghanistan and also names Kanishka. The code pairs items in order when List-II repeats, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Match places first, then the repeated ruler.

x: I, II, III and IV are all correct: the Rabatak inscription lists Saketa, Kaushambi, Pataliputra and Sri Champa among the cities under Kanishka.
t: Recall the cities named at Rabatak.

x: The Sarnath Buddhist image inscription is dated in the third year of Kanishka's reign. The eighth year is the Kalinga War and the twentieth year Ashoka's Lumbini visit.
t: Discriminate the regnal years of different records.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the Prayag Prashasti is called the Allahabad Pillar inscription because it is carved on that pillar, not because it praises Samudragupta.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Harisena wrote the Prayag Prashasti in Sanskrit, in Brahmi script, as a panegyric of Samudragupta, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Separate author, language, script and genre.

x: I, II, III and IV are all correct: the Prayag Prashasti records Samudragupta's political and military success, his southern campaign and the kings of Dakshinapatha he defeated.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: The Mehrauli Iron Pillar was set up as a Vishnu Dhvaja (standard of Vishnu) on the hill called Vishnupada, so it is dedicated to Vishnu.
t: Recall the deity of the pillar.

x: Both are true: the Bhitari pillar of Skandagupta stands in Ghazipur district, and Ghazipur is in Uttar Pradesh.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: The Bhitari pillar records Skandagupta's war against the Hunas, who invaded the Gupta empire. The Cholas, Pandyas and Pratiharas belong to other periods.
t: Recall the enemy of Skandagupta.

x: All five are correct: the Mandsaur (Dashpur) inscription in Malwa dates from Kumaragupta I's reign, names Governor Bandhuvarman and records the silk weavers called Tantuvayas.
t: Check each detail separately.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Nagabhata I was a Gurjara-Pratihara ruler by dynasty, while his defeat of a Mlechchha (Arab) army is a separate achievement.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true: the Mlechchha ruler defeated by Nagabhata I is taken to be an Arab ruler of Sindh, and this victory is recorded in the Gwalior inscription.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: The Aihole inscription of Pulakeshin II is at Aihole in Bagalkot district, Karnataka. Allahabad, Mandsaur and Ghazipur hold other inscriptions.
t: Recall the location of each inscription.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the Aihole inscription is in Sanskrit and uses Southern Brahmi, but a script does not determine the language.
t: Discriminate language from script.

x: I, II, III and IV are all correct: Aihole names the Gurjaras, Harsha and Kalidasa, while the Lohnara inscription of Pulakeshin II does not mention Harsha.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: The Badami rock inscription belongs to Pulakeshin I and Lohnara to Pulakeshin II; Sondani was composed by Vasula Kavi for Yashodharman. The item is doubtful: Sondani appears twice in List-I, so options B and D both fit and only the code order favours D.
t: Match the Chalukya kings first.

x: Both are true: the Maukhari copper seal, found at Asirgarh Fort in Madhya Pradesh, gives the Maukhari genealogy starting with Harivarman.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the Thanjavur inscription shows Chola expansion overseas because it records Rajaraja I's naval victory over the Chera fleet at Kandalur.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: I, II, III, IV and V are all correct: Thanjavur records the defeat of the Chera fleet, and the long temple-wall inscriptions of Rajaraja I and Rajendra I recording victories make Chola history well documented.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Both are true: Gopala was chosen by the people to end Matsya Nyaya, meaning "law of the fish" or the law of the jungle, the anarchy where the strong ate the weak.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: The Khalimpur inscription records Gopala's selection, Matsya Nyaya means law of the jungle, and the key pairs Dharmapala with "his title" and Param Saugat with Buddhist faith, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iv, d-iii. The item is doubtful: option C (Dharmapala-Buddhist, Param Saugat-title) fits equally well.
t: Match the clear pairs, then compare the last two.

x: All twelve are listed in the Kakatiya Motupalli epigraph: sandal, camphor, rose water, ivory, pearls, corals, copper, zinc, lead, silk, pepper and areca nuts.
t: Recall the goods in the tariff list.

x: I, II and III are correct: Motupalli was a trading port, its epigraph fixes commodity tariffs and shows imports and exports. IV is false because famine relief belongs to the Mahasthan inscription.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Govinda III was a Rashtrakuta king, both the Sanjan and Radhanpur plates belong to him, and the Gurjara-Pratiharas were the dynasty he defeated. The code pairs items in order when List-II repeats, giving a-i, b-ii, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Recall the dynasty and records of Govinda III.

x: Both are true: the Sanjan and Radhanpur plates record Govinda III's victory over Nagabhata II, who was a Gurjara-Pratihara king.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Balban's Garhmukteshwar inscription is in the mosque at Garhmukteshwar. Asirgarh Fort holds the Maukhari seal and the Udayagiri caves the Hathigumpha inscription.
t: Link each record to its location.

x: The Rummindei pillar says Ashoka visited Lumbini when he had been consecrated twenty years. The eighth year and 261 BC refer to the Kalinga War.
t: Discriminate Ashoka's regnal-year events.

x: The Sohgaura plate is Mauryan, the Junagadh inscription is at Girnar in Gujarat, Rudradaman repaired the Sudarshan Lake without forced labour, and the Hathigumpha inscription is in the Udayagiri caves of Odisha, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the period or location of each item.

x: Both are true: Kharavela belonged to the Chedi (Mahameghavahana) dynasty, and his Hathigumpha inscription is in the Udayagiri caves near Bhubaneswar, Odisha.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: I, II and III are all correct: the Chausath Yogini temple inscription at Mitaoli in Morena, Madhya Pradesh, is of the Kachchhapaghata dynasty and credits Devapala with building the temple.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: The Hathigumpha inscription records Kharavela's gifts to Jain monks, including caves on Kumari hill. Buddhist monks are the trap.
t: Recall Kharavela's Jain patronage.
